utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, we'll then continue with the examination of the witness, but we first should turn into closed session in order to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Witness GRM097.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that your still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. And the full Bench is present again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the end of the day, we looked at a cable yesterday from Yasushi Akashi dated 16 August 1994 talking about weapon collection points and with a protocol that was attached and we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Today I'd like to take a look at P631 in e-court. And I have a hard copy also that we could give to the witness with the assistance of the usher after showing again to counsel. It's the same document from yesterday but I have now the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what is the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have blank screens on our sides. I don't know if that's what Your Honours have as well. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- let me just have a look. Yes, in e-court I have the English version before me but not on my other screen, and I see that others do have it in both versions. But not for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still don't have any version, but I also see it on other screens it's different in this courtroom. Well, I see a few here. But those who are most in need of looking at the document don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. We also have a black screen, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll seek the assistance of technicians or one technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do have one more hard copy that I could give to my colleagues in the Prosecution so at least they have it. And then I leave it up to Your Honours whether we should wait or proceed since these are my last questions and I can't move to another area, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see that. For us, the disadvantage is that we can't have then -- if we have it in e-court on our screens, we can't follow the transcript and that's important for us as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, something appeared on the left screen, although not what we expected. English versions will be printed out for the time being. The witness has it before him. Mr. Ivetic, I take it that you have a copy before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you have a copy before you as well? Then let's proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what you have in front of you and hopefully the rest of us will have shortly in front of us is dated 12 September 1994. It is from Akashi UNPROFOR Zagreb to Annan Nations New York and it talks about weapons collections points and discusses the prior document we looked at yesterday dated 16 August 1994 with the protocol. And in the -- first of all, sir, have you had a chance to review this document a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to this document, it says in the third paragraph the last lines: "The Bosnian Serb side nevertheless reserved its right to take adequate measures of self-defence in case of attack by the other side. We did not endorse their position." And then the document goes on to say that the protocol that was attached to the prior memo has no legal standing. Now, having read this document, sir, based upon your recollection, knowledge, and understanding of the weapon collection points, what comments do you have about the assertions in this letter about the right to self-defence not being endorsed by the UN?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this (redacted)

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) And this letter is totally not in principle with what was agreed on that day. The whole reason why the weapons collection points were established was because of legitimate Bosnian Serb fears that if the other side broke the agreement, their advantage particularly in infantry would mean that they could quickly overrun territory controlled by what -- the Bosnian Serb army without the heavy weapons to support any counter-attack. And so for that reason, as I said yesterday, the Bosnian government side wanted (redacted)

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) agreed on the 20-kilometre zone. But to satisfy the concerns, which were legitimate concerns, of the Bosnian Serb army, this is why we established a series of weapons zones -- weapon collections points around Sarajevo so that if attacked - and that was if attacked - that they could then defend themselves. Which, again, it was in the spirit of Article 60 of the Geneva Convention which was attached to the UN Security Council Resolution on the establishment of safe areas, which, of course, Sarajevo was a safe area. And therefore, if attacked, the party that was attacked therefore was no longer bound by the demilitarised aspect of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one other matter that we need to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session briefly for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to pause between question and answer, and make sure that they're not too fast in order for the interpretation to be accurate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's perfectly clear. We should follow the strong suggestion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of the Defence team I thank you for answering questions these last two days for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the conclusion of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Witness GRM097, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Edgerton. You find Ms. Edgerton to your right. Ms. Edgerton, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to start with something that you spoke about later on in your evidence yesterday, and if I can just have your indulgence for a moment to see the transcript of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a message that the microphone should be shut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd forgotten that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence. That's why I asked for indulgence earlier. Perhaps -- just a moment, please. Yes, if we could move into private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, I was mistaken. I think we'll need to stay in private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are not in open session for a long time because we take a break. We'll first move into closed session so as to make the protective measures effective, and we'll resume in 20 minutes. And we'll start in closed session in order to allow the witness to enter the courtroom. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I remind both the witness and you, Ms. Edgerton - by the way, also myself - that there should be a break between question and answer, and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just by way of an introduction, I want to move on to another area now that took up a substantial part of our time yesterday, and that's the shelling of the market-place in Sarajevo on 5 February 1994. Now, to begin with, you accept, don't you, that the blast that killed so many and injured so many more on the 5th of February was caused by a single mortar shell, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the analysis said, yes. That's the accepted version of what happened. There were other conspiracy theories but that's the conclusion that was drawn, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked about what you accept, not what others accept --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You accept that. So, therefore, the other theories are not yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you have never conducted a crater analysis; correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you -- you're -- you didn't know that, just on top of that, that this wasn't an isolated incident that day at all, and, in fact, that UNMOs that day had confirmed 55 mixed impacts coming into Bosnian-held areas and zero outgoing. You're not aware of that, are you?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that is in reference to P7538, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you can't read a mortar firing table; correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your experience is originally as an antitank officer?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's also correct that you have never reviewed the specific findings of the UN expert commission that was convened by Ambassador Akashi?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge of any local or other technical investigations that might have been conducted into the incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: GRM097 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness GRM097, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. Before you leave this courtroom, we'll go into closed session as to make the protective measures effective. And I take it that we'll -- after the break, that we'll resume in open session and that will be in 20 minutes from now. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I would only be asked to excused also while we're in closed session so I can go do other tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Witness, you may follow the usher once we are in closed session. We turn into closed session. And we take a break until ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The microphone is open.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, good afternoon. Two follow-up exhibit issues. We've uploaded new versions of the two Assembly sessions that I'd used on Monday. First, we've uploaded 65 ter 02362C, which includes the portion of the 22nd Assembly Session already admitted as P7196, and also Ms. Plavsic's remarks were used on Monday. If the Defence doesn't object, we'd ask that the court officer be instructed to replace P7196 with 65 ter 02362C and that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Lukic? Not at this moment. But you know always within 48 hours you have an opportunity to revisit the matter. Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the present version of P7196 by the newly uploaded one as just referred to by Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. Was P7196, was it marked for identification only? If so, we have to decide on admission. If it was already --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When I enter it into Ring-Tail, the exhibit status I get is EXH. But it was initially marked during the testimony of, I think, Witness Solaja to make a selection and then it was used again with Witness Sokanovic that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But present status --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But my understanding is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask Madam Registrar to confirm what the present status is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has exhibit status. Therefore replacement of the content is sufficient and we don't have to need a further decision on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. But first I think I would like to say, Mr. Kijac, welcome back in court. We were dealing with a few procedural matters when you entered the courtroom. I leave it in Mr. Lukic's hands at this moment, whether he needs to do something which really can't wait until a later moment, and then I would ask a bit of patience. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I spoke with Mr. Traldi, and for him to be able to plan his cross-examination, we agreed that I should offer associated exhibits into evidence what I forgot to do yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yesterday. The day before --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we have to deal with that first, Mr. Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So maybe Ms. Registrar could associate numbers. There is a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, for the associated exhibits have you prepared already a list and have you assigned numbers, or are you in a position to assign numbers now? Yes ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We didn't prepare Madam Registrar for this proceeding. We talk among each other. And maybe Mr. Traldi just can say if he has any objections and then we can assign the numbers later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We have, as set out in our 92 ter response, only an objection to one which is 65 ter 1D05433. That was denied as an associated exhibit in the Karadzic case, denied admission in the context of the same statement, the same document, and in the absence of any compelling reason, we suggest that it also be denied here. When numbers are assigned, I'd just -- Mr. Lukic made a correction to the annex to their filing on Monday and the assignment should refer to 04068 rather than 09661 consistent with the correction he made on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then proceed already on the basis of knowing that there are no objections apart from this one. And whatever the Karadzic Chamber may have decided, of course, that's not in any way binding upon us. We may not even fully know why they denied it and we'll make our own assessment, our own judgement on admissibility. But that being clear, I think we could continue at this moment. Madam Registrar will then further prepare a list, perhaps not yet include that one contested associated exhibit, and we proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just to clarify our position, Your Honour, I certainly hadn't suggested that the Trial Chamber simply unthinkingly adopt what another Chamber had done, but to suggest that, in our submission, the document is not integral and indispensable to the understanding of the witness's statement and so should be denied as it was in that previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. Then please proceed. Mr. Kijac, we'll now -- again we'll further hear your testimony rather than to bore you with all kind of administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you again that you'll still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of -- apparently there is a -- is the volume okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you first check whether everything is okay there. Yes? Okay. It works again, so I remind you again that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing butt truth. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now I want to turn today to your evidence about events in Sarajevo in 1992. In paragraphs 16 through 19 of your statement, you describe the barricades which were set up in Sarajevo in early March 1992. You say you don't know that the SDS had a Crisis Staff at the Holiday Inn hotel that day and you were at your office the whole time. Have I correctly understood your evidence on this point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received the evidence of a Defence witness named Nedjo Vlaski. You knew him personally; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was a co-worker of yours in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1992, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: He was a co-worker of yours, first, in the SNB of the RS MUP during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a decision for him at the MUP. But you're talking about March 1992. At that time, I was the secretary of the city SUP, and as far as I know, Nedjo Vlaski at the time was in the security service of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vlaski, your co-worker during the war, testified at transcript page 27790 that you were at the Holiday Inn at the time the barricades were set up. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I was outside of Sarajevo when the barricades were set up, and I found out about them only in the evening at about 9.00 p.m. And once I learnt that the barricades were erected, I managed to enter the city secretariat. That's where I spent the night. I wasn't at the Holiday Inn, and I didn't leave the office until the situation was -- let me put it this way, was normalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So Mr. Vlaski, in your submission, is lying that you were at the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. "Lying" we, first, don't use in this courtroom. Second, it doesn't mean that he can have the other impression. Lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Traldi, you wanted to ask the witness, I take it, that this witness contests the truth of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And please choose your words in this way yourself --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you then contest the truth of Mr. Vlaski's testimony that you were at the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Vlaski said. I can confirm that the entire time I spent at my office at the city Secretariat of the Interior, that I had two of my assistants with me. Mr. Leotar was a crimes assistant and Mr. Redzep Adzic was the police assistant. I didn't leave anywhere until the situation was normalised. I think remained there for 24 hours directly managing the action from my office. I don't know about Mr. Vlaski. Perhaps he was there, and it's possible that he has his own impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 03838. Now this is an interview with Momcilo Mandic published in Slobodna Bosna in 1998. If we could turn to page 4 in both languages, and if we could zoom in on the middle of the page in the B/C/S at the bottom under [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic is asked about the barricades. He says Krajisnik and Karadzic were in Belgrade. He refers to the Gardovic killing. And then he says towards the end of the paragraph: Rajko Djukic headed the committee for the organisation of barricades. I do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, please, slowly reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll start that sentence again: "Rajko Djukic headed the committee for the organisation of barricades. I do not wish to hide anything. Dragan Kijac, Mico Stanisic, myself, and some others from the MUP took part in this, and we organised everything so as to avoid bloodshed and to show to the public and Izetbegovic they could not act like that ..." So you also organised -- took part in organising the barricades; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. The very text says differently than the proposal, that this gentleman did everything to prevent bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no discussions about that. You, Mr. Lukic, if you think that Mr. Traldi is misquoting any statement, whether he quotes it in a context which is the one you'd like to hear about is a different matter. Then you can say, Please quote literally and then that will be done. And just as you sometimes select certain portions you want to put to the witness, that is what Mr. Traldi is allowed to do as well. So if there is any inaccuracy in the quoting, Mr. Traldi should take care of that. Other things have to remain until re-examination. Is there any problem with the words quoted or a summary which is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have B/C/S version in front of me and I think that it basically is the same as in English. I think that the context is completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Context is fine. Then you can clarify that in re-examination. The only thing we're concerned about at this moment is whether there is any misquote or an inaccurate summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the truth is that, like Mr. Mandic says here, you took part in organising the barricades; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, my only problem with your line of questioning is that we don't see in this passage that this witness was at the Holiday Inn on that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- I agree, Your Honour, and I framed the question carefully this time that he took part in organising the barricades. And so what I'm putting to him this time is that what Mr. Mandic said in the interview is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I'm trying to suggest is that question that you are now putting is a shift from the first question and I'm not sure whether indeed we're still pursuing the truthfulness or lack of truthfulness of this witness who testified earlier or whether you're now going into a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to make it implicitly clear, Your Honour, the case that I'm putting to the witness is that his description of his role in these events is contradicted on multiple points by multiple sources who knew him and had no incentive to do anything other than tell the truth about his role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to briefly repeat my question, the truth, like Mr. Mandic says here, is that you took part in organising the barricades; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Traldi. I came as the city secretary on the 24th of February, so it was some days before the barricades. The barricades were erected when the Serbian best man was killed. I think that was on the 1st of March, seven days after I took up my duties. I know that Mr. Mandic participated in the barricades and that Mr. Nedjo Vlaski had a self-inflicted injury there. But I did not take part in the organisation of the barricades and I was not at the Holiday Inn at the time. I didn't even know that the Crisis Staff, or however you call it, was in session at the Holiday Inn. And since I was not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, I did not have any contacts with the Serbian Democratic Party or with the people who -- such as Rajko Dukic who are mentioned here and who were involved in that. On the other hand, at the time you could not move around Sarajevo. It was unsafe. There were both Serbian and Muslim barricades. I did not go to see my family for 24 hours, Mr. Traldi, never mind walk around. There were two barricades very close my apartment, one was a Serbian one, one was a Muslim one. There was firing from there, and other than by telephone, I was not able to contact my family. So then I went to see my family [as interpreted] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you've now gone well beyond my question. I'm going to ask you to focus on the question that I directly ask you. During the course of your answer you said you did not have any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think there is some mistake either in translation or transcribing. The gentleman did not say that he went to see his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, he did not. He said he did not, at least that's what I heard, did not go to see his family. But the issue was not whether there were barricades and what effect they had on the witness. The issue and the question was about whether this witness participated in organising them. That was the issue, but I think everyone understood that the witness said that and certainly the transcript will --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. In 65, line 7, it says: "Then I went to see my family," and he didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We heard, and I put that on the record a second ago, that we heard he did not go and see his family for such a time, and that will be worked -- I mean, the transcript is not the final one yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in any case, at line 3 he says: "I did not go to see my family for 24 hours ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it seems that it's a minor issue on the whole matter and it will be corrected anyhow. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you say -- you said in your last answer you did not have any contacts with the Serbian Democratic Party. In fact, as you say in paragraph 11 of your statement, your appointment in Sarajevo was approved by Radovan Karadzic; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's not in dispute, Mr. Traldi, but we cannot link him up with this at the time. There was a tripartite authority, a coalition of three parties, and a few days after this authority was set up Mr. Karadzic called me. That has nothing to do with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're being asked by the interpreters to slow down and by me, again, to focus directly on the question that I ask you, which is not about the tripartite system or the history of the government. As you told us on Monday, you're not a politician; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I did not have any contacts with the Serbian Democratic Party other than meetings with Mr. Karadzic in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move on, but before I do I'll tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03838 receives Exhibit Number P7585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P3009. And I'm turning now to the beginning of April -- end of March/beginning of April 1992 and the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you had no information about the division of the MUP except for a dispatch from Momcilo Mandic. Now this is that dispatch; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so. There's no need for me to read it. We don't need to lose too much time, Mr. Traldi. I assume that that is that dispatch. It's addressed to, among others, the SUP Sarajevo, personally to me. We don't need to check what's in it right now. We don't want to lose time with me having to read the content of the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, leave it in Mr. Traldi's hands what he considers is worth to use time on. Mr. Traldi -- listen to his questions and please answer them. If he asks you to read it, you'll read it. If he doesn't ask, then -- but to be sure that this is the dispatch, you might -- you had a look at it, you say it is, even without having read it in its totality again. That's how I understood your testimony. Can you confirm it is or do you need more time to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say you spent a weekend in early April 1992 in Pale municipality. You mention you went to Podgrab village and the Pale SJB. Did you also go to the scout's hall while you were in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you permit me, Mr. Traldi, I said this and I think I said in my statement that on Friday afternoon I went to Pale with my family, that I was stopped by a Muslim barricade at the exit to Sarajevo held by the Green Berets and the police, and that I was also stopped again in Serb territory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was whether you also went to the scout's hall. And by the first word - no - you've answered that question. Whatever you did, if there's any reason to further explore that, Mr. Lukic will do it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Had you visited the scout's hall at all in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Scout's hall, I'm sorry, I don't really know what that is. In the beginning, it was translated to me as the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm thinking of a place called Kalovita Brda in Pale.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never at that building, unless you're thinking of the MUP building in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33291. Now this is part of Milan Scekic's testimony in the Stanisic-Zupljanin case. If we can scroll down -- we have the whole page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So he's asked when he first became aware of talk within the MUP about forming a Serbian MUP. He says: "The first time I heard of it was in 1992" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line are we at?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: His answer begins at line 17, Your Honour. He says in late March or early April. He says he came out into the street and met two of his colleagues, he cannot recall their names. They asked me if I wanted to join them on their way to Pale. I did, he says, and Mico Stanisic Dragan Kijac, and chiefs of public security from Sarajevo municipalities were present, as well as the representatives of the ten peripheral municipalities. If we could turn to page 3 at the bottom. It says, he is asked: "Mr. Witness, my question is: The meeting in Pale that you talked about where in Pale was the meeting held, if you remember?" He answers: "It was held at Kalovita Brda, formally known as the scout's hall. The meeting was brief. We were given the information and parted ways." If we can turn to the top of page 4, he is asked: "Do you recall who led or chaired the meeting?" He says: "I think it was Dragan Kijac who chaired the meeting ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to whether you chaired a meeting at Kalovita Brda in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand which building you're referring to. It's the MUP building. It was the MUP building. I don't know what it was used for earlier on. In April 1992, a ministry was established there, the Ministry of the Interior was there. So it wasn't a scout's hall or a sports hall. As far as Mr. Scekic is concerned, well, this must have happened a lot later. He went to Sarajevo at least a month and a half or two after the conflict had broken out, and for that reason, he had unpleasant experiences. So it's quite possible that he thought it was in May or June. But for me to be the chairman of the meeting, well, at the time I could only have been the chairman within my own service. I wasn't the head of the service, Mr. Skipina was, as well as Mr. Mico Stanisic. But I was in Kalovita Brda throughout the period of April. I do apologise, but I had to provide you with some detail in order to describe the relative context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you contest, just to cut it short, the truthfulness of his testimony that you chaired meetings about the establishment of the RS MUP at Kalovita Brda at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should just ... maybe the rest of this paragraph should be read in all the fairness to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is suggested to you, Mr. Traldi. If you follow that suggestion, please do so. If you don't follow it, then Mr. Lukic will have an opportunity to further deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to finish the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, one thing I noticed, I don't know whether there comes down in the next paragraph, but you used the plural, "meetings." Whereas I think from what was read it was "a meeting."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll phrase very precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Or I'll attempt to anyway, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Scekic's full answer is: "I think it was Dragan Kijac who chaired the meeting. I believe Mico Stanisic was present as well. Of course, this was 18 years ago, I may be mistaken, but I would really like to give a fair statement true to what I experienced and what I remember. But I believe this was the case, that Dragan Kijac chaired the meeting and that Mico Stanisic was present." Do you also contest the truthfulness of Mr. Scekic's sworn testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Scekic said that this what he thought. I have no reason to dispute this, but -- I can't lead a meeting as minister of the interior. Mico Stanisic would have had to open the meeting and maybe given me the floor. But for me to lead a meeting, to chair a meeting, that wasn't quite the way things were organised within the Ministry of the Interior. Especially because I was the head of the sector at the time, Mr. Traldi. So I was only the head of the sector at the time and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So thus far, Mr. Vlaski, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Scekic have all misremembered your activities at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in doubt as to whether or not they can remember this correctly, but I can remember what the case was better. I don't say that I wasn't at Kalovita Brda and that I spent the entire period of April there. There was an office there about the third of the size of this area, so it wasn't anyone else's office, it was a hall for meetings because the ministry didn't have any room at the time. It was a hall, a room that the 10 or 15 of us would use. We were sitting there at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you. I hadn't asked for a description of the room. I'd put a fairly straightforward question, I think, and I'd just ask you again to focus on it. Now, you became aware that there were no or very few non-Serb personnel in the RS MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time in Pale, yes, it's quite certain that there were no non-Serbs. As for other areas, I don't know. I can speak about the situation up until August. In the State Security Service there were mainly Serbs from the Ministry of Interior or from the State Security Service that I was in charge of. On the whole, they were Serbs. There were no non-Serbs. As for other organisational units in the field, I do believe that there were people from other ethnicities, Muslims and Croats. They worked in certain organisational units. I know some of them and I know some of them who remained there until the end of the war. But I can only tell you what I am aware of, that is, the State Security Service. There were no non-Serbs there. Because the Serbs who had left Sarajevo started establishing a State Security Service in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33278. And as it comes up, I will ask that the witness be given 90(E) advice at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, Mr. Traldi has invited me to make you acquainted with Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And I'll read it to you. The rule says: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." So if you fear that a truthful answer would incriminate yourself, you may address me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now these are the minutes of the expanded session of the expert collegium held on 10 and 11 of November, 1993, in Pale. If we could turn to page 3 in both languages, we see the beginning of the meeting. And at page 4, both languages, in the second paragraph, we see that it begins: "The following persons were present at the session, which was chaired on 10 November 1993 by Dragan Kijac, and on 11 November 1993, by the acting minister, Tomo Kovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now in light of your answers about the collegium on Monday, before I move on, I just want to make sure, would you have been psychologically present or psychologically absent while you were chairing the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having chaired a meeting of the Ministry of the Interior with these individuals. So that didn't correspond to my level of job description. So I'm quite surprised by this. This is the first time I have seen things being formulated in this way. I can't have chaired a meeting of the Ministry of the Interior which included assistants for public safety who had the same status as I did, if not an even higher status.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at the bottom of the page we read: "After expounding the agenda, Dragan Kijac opened the discussion on the first item." Now, you've been to enough meetings to know that's the chair's role. It's not just a random guy at the meeting who expounds the agenda and opens the discussion; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I would say this is quite impossible. I can see that it says Dragan Kijac chaired the meeting, but if you have look at those who attended the meeting, well, I don't have any responsibility for assistants for finance, for assistants for communications, for [indiscernible], for the chief of -- the Chef de Cabinet Radomir Milos. I really cannot be the chairman of such a meeting involving such individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you don't -- you say you were not there. You did not chair that meeting. You did not chair that meeting. Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said. But as to whether I was at the meeting, I probably was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear. But you don't have to explain always why your answer is the right answer. I mean, to say it's impossible that it was otherwise unless there's some clear physical impossible. But just arguing about why your recollection must be the right one is not something that is important for us at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in fact --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. But I get carried away. Because this is the first time I have seen this today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, wait for the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we can have page 8 in the English and the bottom of page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see in the next-to-last paragraph in the B/C/S and in the middle of the page in English, that Stojan Zupljanin explained his proposal for giving what's translated as work contracts to employees of non-Serb ethnicity, stating that he had taken as the main criteria the meeting of general and specific conditions. He mentioned, in particular, that over 400 journalists and 120 TV crew who had visited Banja Luka last year were interested specifically in those persons. Now it's fair to say that what he is interested in is achieving public relations benefits, right, by hiring non-Serbs? That's what he's proposing; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had this in mind a while ago when answering your question. In certain centres, there were employees who were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in B/C/S and it will be the second paragraph. First full paragraph, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What we read there is that Dragan Kijac, Andrija Bjelosevic, Krsto Savic, and Milenko Karisik were opposed to Zupljanin's proposal, while Goran Macar stressed that no such people could work at the forensic department while the war was ongoing. Now, that's your position as you articulated it to the collegium; right? You were opposed to hiring non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no hiring, Mr. Traldi. These people worked in the service before the war. They just remained on and worked in the Ministry of the Interior. They weren't new employees, you understand? Before 1992, before the war broke out, they worked in the Ministry of the Interior. They remained there and some of them continued to work there until the end of the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the other hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I've asked you about is your position. Your position as you articulated to the collegium on this occasion was you were opposed to giving contracts to non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, it's the same thing again. These are people who worked in the Ministry of the Interior before the war. These people were not new people. As for my opinion, I can't express it to the head of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin, because I have no authority over Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about answering the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you opposed to Stojan Zupljanin's proposal which was read out by Mr. Traldi a second ago? Were you opposed to that? That's the simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't be for or against this proposal because that did not concern my field of activity, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand, then, that's what's recorded here as your position as expressed during that meeting, that that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it is correct. This was drafted as if I had been the chairman, so I don't think it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's wrongly recorded. That's your position. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you say this can't be correct because it was drafted as if you had been the chairman. If Minister Kovac wasn't present, one of his two under-secretaries would chair the meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, you have to understand how the Ministry of the Interior was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm not asking for a long explanation of the ministry's organisation. I'm asking you about if Minister Kovac wasn't present at the collegium meeting who would chair it, and what I'm putting to you is it would have been one of the under-secretaries; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The state security couldn't have a meeting at which there were public employees. You can see that there wasn't a single state employee. How could I have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you were invited to repeat your answer. I leave it to you, Mr. Lukic, whether -- where everyone was about, I think, to try to get the witness back to the question, whether there's any need to do that. You have listened to it, I take it, in B/C/S. Witness, could you please answer the questions rather than explain all kind of things without answering the question. The question was, and you did it very briefly, that it would not be -- if Minister Kovac wasn't there, that it would not be two of the under-ministers who would replace him. Then the simple question is: Who would replace him if he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't know. Minister Kovac wasn't a minister. That's the first thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Kovac was not there, you wouldn't know who would replace him, apart from whether he was a minister or not. That's an answer to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You just said Minister Kovac wasn't a minister. Is it your evidence now that you don't recall who was the acting minister of the interior in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to whether he was a -- in an acting position or not, I don't know. There was someone called Ratko Hadzic and there was a sort of vacuum at the time. I don't think that Mr. Kovac was the acting minister, if my memory doesn't fail me, and I think it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move on, but before I do, I will tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 33278 receives Exhibit Number P7586, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7586 is admitted into -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I do not have objection for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only we would [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would like to know how this document was obtained by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if you could answer the question right away it would be appreciated. Otherwise inform Mr. Lukic at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's being checked but we'll answer no later than the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 49 of your statement, sir, turning to a new topic, you say that as of late June and early July 1995, the RDB was focused mostly on the Sarajevo-Trnovo theatre of war. That means that you would have been monitoring events that theatre; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me which paragraph you are referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 49. And while you look for it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can already inform Mr. Lukic that the last document was seized from the RS MUP CJB Srpsko Sarajevo in Pale in June 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you were monitoring events in the Sarajevo-Trnovo theatre in late June and early July, if your attention was focused there, you would have been monitoring events there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, given the information that I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you'd have been monitoring forces deployed there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which forces do you have in mind? There's quite some distance between Sarajevo and Trnovo. If you are referring to Trnovo or are you referring to the Sarajevo theatre of war? Could you try and be more precise? I'm not quite sure which forces you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. If a new unit was deployed to Trnovo while your attention was focused on it at that time, that's something that wouldn't have escaped your attention; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I've asked you about this. The Trnovo theatre of war, when conflicts broke out in the Trnovo theatre of war, we had an operative who went there from Sarajevo and he monitored the situation and submitted reports to us about the security situation in that battlefield. So we did have an operative there, on the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to start with the Sarajevo side. Now, you knew at that time - early July 1995 - that in the area of Sarajevo under Muslim control the citizens didn't even have the basic conditions for survival; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite a broad concept. Basic conditions for survival, well, that is quite a broad concept. There's no doubt that the situation in Sarajevo was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have, just, I think, for efficiency, 65 ter 33181.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is an RDB report dated the 2nd of July, 1995, bearing your name and sent personally to the deputy minister of the interior and the head of the public security department. If we can turn to page 2 in both languages, and it's the third paragraph in the English, we read -- and it's the first full paragraph in the B/C/S: "We are in possession of information that the situation in the area of Sarajevo which is under Muslim control continues to worsen owing to the lack of the basic conditions for survival. For these reasons, citizens have started to abandon the town, passing through the tunnel at their own risk." Now, this was what you knew to be the truth about the situation in Sarajevo at the beginning of July 1995 when your attention was focused on that theatre; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch shows this was an intercepted conversation between two individuals and one can see that they were commenting on this. The comments were conveyed, were relayed, the comments made in that intercepted conversation, it says, on the basis of the comments made by two Muslims. So it is obvious that this conversation was intercepted and this paragraph was drafted on the basis of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the information that you had that you were reporting to the department minister of the interior and to the top of the CJB -- sorry, the top of the SJB, the public security side, was that there's a lack of basic conditions for survival in the Muslim-controlled area of Sarajevo; right? That's what you report up in this document? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But could we please go back to the first page. The 2nd of July, 1995, is the date of this dispatch. As early as the 15th of June there were hundreds of documents that mentioned offensives launched from Sarajevo against our positions. If the situation had been so catastrophic, a large-scale offensive wouldn't have been launched against the Serbian positions. The offensive had already lasted for 20 days by that time. You have scores of documents about this matter. We could have a look at them. I don't know. When you are preparing yourself, you probably saw that in mid-June an offensive was launched in Sarajevo, against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I tender the document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, you said, sir, Mr. Traldi, that it bears the witness's name. Can we see where it bears his name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have the end of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 33181 receives Exhibit Number P7587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. I have one question. What you're saying is - at least if I understood you well - that the situation was, of course, not defined by what you find here. Now, not in this way does this report say: Ignore this because it's not the real situation, which we heard to the contrary. It says what you can infer from that situation. So I'm a bit puzzled by your answer saying, Well, this was reported as reflecting relevant factual information to the minister, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Orie, at that time we did not have such a clear view of Sarajevo to be able to know things. This is an intercepted conversation. We include it, but we don't have the option of verifying it out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask: Where does it state that this is an intercept, from this document? I'm a bit lost here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the basis of comments by two Muslims, it can clearly be concluded. So these are comments. In overviews such as this, you don't see the source of the information. When you receive the dispatch from Sarajevo, then you can conclude what the source of information was. This is just an overview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The comments of the two Muslims refers to no army success in Hadzici. It doesn't say anything about basic conditions of survival not being present. And in any case, even though -- even if it were referring to that, it doesn't show that this is an intercept. I'm just asking where do we see that this is an intercept? You could have heard Muslims talking to you. That's not an intercept, they're just talking to you. Where do we find in this document that this is an intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Information such as this, you will not get the source of the information. You will see that many things are referred to here. Gojko Susak, what he thinks, then comments by two Muslim citizens, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question, sir, I'm sorry. You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying, I'm trying to answer you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, just show me in this document where we see that this is an intercept. Don't tell me about Gojko somebody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot see that from this document. No one can see it from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi. No, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do have one quick follow-up, but I'll save it for after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that. Witness, we'll take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. That's 25 minutes to 2.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see that you only need a few seconds even. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President. Thank you. This is in reference to the Defence motion filed on the 8th of October to add witnesses to its 65 ter list. The Prosecution does not oppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I'll deal briefly with another procedural matter. Madam Registrar has prepared a list of the associated exhibits which are not contested, which are not in dispute, and has assigned numbers to them. That list will be filed this afternoon. And hereby the Chamber admits into evidence D1300 up to and including D1320, and the corresponding numbers are to be found on the list that will be filed this afternoon by Madam Registrar. And again, the one objected to is not included in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kijac, we'll continue. May I urge you again to focus your answer on what was asked. If any further explanation is needed, either by Mr. Traldi or later by Mr. Lukic, they'll ask for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, sticking with the document in front of us, before the break you said the source of the information contained in this report you can conclude that when you received the dispatch from Sarajevo. That dispatch from Sarajevo is the dispatch that the regional national security centre sent to the head office; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And on the basis of the various regional dispatches, you and your team would draft the daily report to send to the deputy minister and the head of the public security sector; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you would choose what information from the regional reports to provide to the deputy minister; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either myself or the chief of analysis, all would receive documents in their sphere of work, the papers, and then they would mark for analysis parts that were interesting. And then the analysis sector would draft a report like this one which would -- which then I would sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you and your team would not -- let me start the question again. You and your team would provide to the deputy minister information that you found important, information you found reliable; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would provide -- well, if I may be a little bit broader, Your Honours, to explain to Mr. Traldi. Perhaps we would receive 100 pieces of information from the field. What you can see, perhaps 20 of them could be used, 80 per cent would not be interesting, but the 20 would be used to draft a document like this. At that point, we would not know how reliable the information was. It was war, you know. We did not have the support in order to be able to monitor any area. We would accept what the operative would send from the field, but we would not have the opportunity to verify it. We would send it like that. Perhaps -- here's an example, if the Court would permit me, I could be a bit more detailed. We get information that a sabotage group infiltrate a certain area. They would say information was available. We would pass that on. This information would not necessarily have to be true. We would be obliged to warn the military intelligence organ that this could possibly happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But you certainly wouldn't include it if you knew or believed it to be false; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the option once I received the paper to verify it. You understand? All I would look for is to see whether it was something important or not important. I didn't have the opportunity to verify it because every day something new would happen. In peacetime when he would send information like this to me, I would react in an instructional way. Because, in the service, we would also be providing instructions, so then we would order them to do such and such a thing to verify information. But at this point, from day to day, when things were happening like that, you didn't have the chance to verify this information. Perhaps I can take an example from those documents. In one of our informations, it would say that so many Muslims escaped from Pilica, let's say. Later I read a report done by the international forces and they established that this was not so, but we did include it in one of these information reports. We passed it on, but we didn't know whether this was a verified piece of information or not. It was up to us to ring the alarm at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's a rather long explanation of how it worked. But if you had some doubts, you would express that in a report, isn't it, or if you would have some doubts on whether it was reliable or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have that kind of insight, whether something was verified or not, whether it was suspicious or not. I just would get the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I take you to page 1 of this document. Almost at the bottom, in English at least, I don't know where it is in -- yes, I think it's also the semi-last paragraph. It says: "According to unverified information, a member of UNPROFOR has reported that there were about," this and this and this. So isn't it true that your answer just a second ago squarely contradicts what we find here in the report, that if there were reasons to make clear that it was unverified, and you would do that if there is doubt, isn't it, that you would put that in the report. You said you couldn't do that, but I see that it was done in the report. Do you have an explanation for that? A short explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would depend on the dispatch. This dispatch that came regarding 5.000 Mujahedin from Islamic countries, it says that it was an unverified piece of information and that is how we would convey it. Where this is stated, then we would also pass it on like that. We would also mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which is not fully consistent with all your previous answers where you didn't make such a -- such a condition. But let's move on. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to the Trnovo part of the Sarajevo-Trnovo theatre. And can we have P345. And this is another of General Mladic's notebooks from the war. If we could have page 209 in the English, 211 in the B/C/S. We see here in the English - and we're just getting the B/C/S - General Mladic's notes of a meeting on 30 June 1995 with Slobodan Milosevic at the VJ General Staff. If we could turn to page 211 in the English, 213 in the B/C/S, we see under Milosevic's initials a discussion of the 5th Corps and then a mention of Krupa. And turning to the next page, at the end of Milosevic's remarks, we read: "Jovica should resolve logistics problems and let the RS resolve this problem of holding up convoys." And then we see someone with the initials JS is recorded as the next speaker in General Mladic's notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, given the level of the meeting and what you've read here, you can tell that JS and Jovica, those refer to your counterpart in DB Serbia, Jovica Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for clear speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's a leading question, that's clear. But the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How many Jovicas with the last initial S can you think of who would have been at a level to attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Where do we see that in JS that it's Jovica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: JS, I think it is -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. First, I'd put to the witness a question, but, second, the basis for my question is that Milosevic says what Jovica should do and then JS is the next speaker. I think that's sufficient to put a question on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the previous sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I given a ruling. The previous sentence is sufficient basis to put the question, not to draw any definitive conclusions. It's sufficient basis for the question. Please proceed. A question which is leading, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you need me to repeat the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a meeting with Mladic and Slobodan Milosevic at the VJ General Staff. How many people with the first name Jovica and the last initial S can you name who as of 30 June 1995 were at a sufficient level of seniority to attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot think along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Try with me. This isn't a casual gathering. It's a meeting at the VJ General Staff. The two people that you know are there are the president of Serbia and the commander of the VRS Main Staff. How many Jovicas -- let me put it to you this way. If this were a piece of information that were coming before you in your work as -- in national security, in your intelligence work, you would act on the basis that the most likely conclusion is that's Jovica Stanisic that's being referred to, wouldn't you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Traldi, this is something that would not come to my desk. Let's understand each other. We were not a service that was monitoring such high-level people. Try to put a question to me and I will try to answer it. First of all, to go into this, I can't even read it. I mean, if you put a question to me, I will reply. I mean, there's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question was put to you, and then you answered that you couldn't think in those lines. Simple question now is: Could you know, could you give us any name of a person by the initials JS who would be in such a position to attend a meeting where Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Mladic would be present? Can you give us any suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be thinking along those lines, Your Honours. At this point, I cannot recall initials, who was the prime minister, who was the president of the republic, and all those different initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If there would have been a person present there by the first name Jovica, and if the last name would be -- would start with an S, would you have any suggestion who that could have been? And Mr. Traldi suggests to that you it may have been Jovica Stanisic. But if you have any other idea of who that could have been, you're invited to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not ruling it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question, whether you could rule it out. My question was whether you could think of any -- witness, the question was whether you could think of any other person by the first name Jovica, last name starting with an S, who would be at such a level that he could attend such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 213 in the English, page 215 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see JS is recorded beginning at the bottom of the page by General Mladic to say: "They should not be engaged (we gave 80 from you Erdut, we gave 80 from Djeletovci ..." Now, you know that DB Serbia had a unit known as the Skorpions based at Djeletovci; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a unit there called the Skorpions, but I don't know who was in charge of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's see if we can refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 06767.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now this is a document coming from General Mladic dated the 1st of July, 1995, the next day, re the telegram of the MUP of Serbia's antiterrorist unit from the 30th of June, 1995. He describes how he should be informed if anyone is seriously wounded in the Trnovo sector. And then turning to the next page in the English, says: "The MUP of the RS in Pale shall notify representatives of the MUP of Serbia and Colonel Golic of our decision." Now, the MUP of Serbia had to be informed about decisions about how information would come about events in the Trnovo sector because there were MUP Serbia forces present there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would comment it like this. I'm seeing this paper for the first time. It's the 1st of July, 1995, and you can see that it's addressed to the RS Pale MUP. At that point in time I was not representing the MUP of Pale. So combat units and what was being used was something that was addressed at the minister of the interior, not to the chief of the department. We don't have units in the field, don't participate in the front. All we do is report what we observe in the field. And up here at the top you can see that this is addressed to the RS Pale MUP, not to the National Security Service. You can look at the information of the Main Staff. That's where it says that it's been sent to me, that it's addressed personally to Dragan Kijac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we may have occasion to look at some of those documents, but at the moment you've answered at least one question but not the one that I asked you. You know based on having an operative in the Trnovo theatre, where you said your attention was focused at the beginning of July 1995, you know there were MUP Serbia forces present there, just like -- or consistent with what General Mladic is writing in this document; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KIJAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to look at the dispatch saying that these forces were there. Could you please show that to me? I don't want to speculate right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You were asked whether you know it. If you know it, tell us; if you don't know it, don't tell us. Don't invite Mr. Traldi to present to you the evidence of what he asks you. Do you -- simple question therefore: Were you aware that there were MUP Serbia forces present there? And we're talking about Trnovo. You were not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
